svg.text: Five claims, and what each one is actually standing on
None of these is wrong. All of them are asserted more strongly than the experiment behind them supports.

g.data-tip: A deletion experiment shows the layers are not redundant. It is not evidence about the direction of the depth-accuracy curve, which is what the sentence is usually quoted for.
g.text: depth is essential
One middle layer deleted costs about 2% top-1;
each conv layer is under 1% of the parameters.
A depth sweep with re-tuning, seeds and
error bars — VGG and ResNet ran it later.

g.data-tip: The baseline is a net with half as many kernels per conv layer, except the last conv and fc layers, left at full size. That makes 1.7% understate the two-GPU net's gain and overstate the split's own: read it as the gain of a bigger net, not of the split topology (slide 10).
g.text: the two-GPU split helps
1.7% top-1 against a one-GPU net with half
the kernels per convolutional layer.
The same full-width net on one card —
the baseline differs in kernels, not just in topology.

g.data-tip: Four hyper-parameters chosen on a validation set, then a gain reported against the version without them. Later work could not reproduce a benefit on ILSVRC at all.
g.text: LRN aids generalization
1.4% top-1, with k, n, α and β themselves
selected on a validation set.
Repeated runs with k, n, α and β
fixed in advance, with error bars.

g.data-tip: The entire ReLU experiment lives on CIFAR-10 with a four-layer network. The paper never measures what the choice of nonlinearity does to ImageNet accuracy.
g.text: ReLU is the better unit
Six times fewer epochs to 25% training error
on a four-layer CIFAR-10 network.
An ImageNet accuracy comparison at
matched compute — never run here.

g.data-tip: The abstract puts 15.3% next to the runner-up's 26.2%. Both are ensembles — the runner-up averages several Fisher-vector classifiers — but two of the seven networks also trained on twelve times more data.
g.text: it beat everyone
15.3% top-5 from seven networks, two with
extra data and an extra convolutional layer.
A single CNN at 18.2% (val) still beats the
26.2% (test) runner-up, itself an ensemble.

svg.text: And the authors' own importance order (§3.1–3.4) has aged badly
Sections 3.1 to 3.4 are sorted, in the authors' words, by their estimation of importance, most important first. The two-GPU split is second, LRN third.
Dropout and the crop augmentation — the two things the paper calls necessary — sit in a later section, and neither is given an error number.
